newsitem.title: FRANCE: France backs Estonia EU membership bid.
newsitem.headline: France backs Estonia EU membership bid.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said after meeting Estonian President Lennart Meri on Thursday that the Baltic state should join the European Union as soon as possible.

"Our views converge on most subjects, notably on membership of the European Union as soon as possible, as Estonia is a country which fulfils practically all the conditions, or is at least one of the first European countries to fulfil the conditions," Chirac told reporters.
Meri outlined "a vision of a future Europe, a Europe which is not a federation but a Europe of different cultures with a common cradle".
Chirac, who has met leaders from several ex-communist states in the past few weeks, has said he backs accession to the EU for Hungary, Poland and Romania.
Both presidents said they had discussed security issues and, according to Chirac, "the concern of Estonia and of Baltic countries to join a security system which gives them all guarantees".

A Chirac spokesman said talks had included NATO enlargement and the need for an accord with Russia in order to guarantee stability. Meri stressed that Russia should not be allowed to veto an agreement.

Estonia, which broke away from the Soviet Union in August 1991, had not been allowed to participate in the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe in November 1990. The last Russian troops left the country in 1994.
The spokesman said Chirac had agreed in principle to a Baltic proposal for a status of association with the Atlantic Alliance.
France has suggested a charter to be agreed between the Alliance and northern countries which are not NATO members -- the three Baltic states but also Finland and Sweden.
Chirac said that he hoped to visit Estonia next year.
Neither leader commented on Estonian Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi's statement on Wednesday that he would resign, which sparked a fresh political crisis.
Leading political parties held emergency talks after Vaehi's announcement, which was prompted by a humiliating no-confidence vote on Monday that he only narrowly won.
Vaehi, who leads Estonia's sixth government since the country quit the former Soviet Union, said he would quit as soon as a new government was formed.
